transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-28 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~39 minutes
Attendees: Alex Marshall (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Jordan Wells (Lumen Eng Manager), Maya Chen (Sr Backend), Samir Patel (Security Lead), Tara Lim (Platform)

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, appreciate you taking the time. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Priya and Diego who'll do most of the tech walkthrough. How's everyone doing?
[00:09] Jordan: Doing good, thanks. We're excited, want to see how quickly our engineers can wire up the SDKs and try a small PoC.
[00:15] Priya: Cool, yep. Today we'll go through the Python quickstart, then a TypeScript example, auth patterns, environment setup, and then cover private deployment / VPC notes that Samir flagged.
[00:25] Samir: yep that's the one, mostly around KMS and audit logs, so we'll ask questions as we go.

-- Python quickstart --
[01:05] Priya: Okay, starting with Python. Install is pip install redwood-inference (there's also a micro package redwood-core for embeddings but we recommend the main package for full features) you'll set REDWOOD_API_KEY as an env var. Example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-xxxxx. We also show a local config file approach in the repo but env var is simplest for CI.
[01:33] Maya: Quick question — do you support rotating keys? Our ops team rotates keys every 30 days.
[01:38] Priya: Yes — API keys are long-lived by default but you can create scoped keys and rotate them. We also support short-lived tokens via the token broker pattern; Diego can follow up with a snippet.
[01:48] Diego: Yeah, for short-lived tokens we provide a small server-side helper in the examples: server issues a signed short token with limited scope, client uses that. It's in the quickstart repo under examples/token-broker.

[02:20] Alex: Priya, walk through a one-shot Python generate call?
[02:24] Priya: Sure. From pseudocode: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.generate(model='rw-large-8k', prompt='Summarize...'); print(resp.text). That's it. We show streaming via client.stream() which yields chunks, and for structured output there's a tool-calling style helper that returns JSON-like structures.
[02:50] Jordan: That model name, rw-large-8k, is that the hosted model or can we point to our private model on dedicated?
[02:57] Priya: Good question; model names map to the catalog. For hosted you pick from our catalog. For Dedicated or Private deployments you pin a model URI — the SDK uses the same client but you set deployment_url or workspace config. There's a config example: REDWOOD_DEPLOYMENT_URL or client = RedwoodClient(endpoint='https://deployments.lumen.redwood.internal', api_key=...).

-- TypeScript quickstart --
[03:30] Diego: For TypeScript it's npm i @redwood/inference, then import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const resp = await client.generate({ model: 'rw-large-8k', input: '...' }); console.log(resp.output); We show both node and browser patterns — for browser you'd use short-lived tokens only.
[04:02] Maya: Do you recommend calling the API from browser? We tend to avoid exposing keys.
[04:07] Diego: We strongly recommend not shipping long-lived keys to the browser. Use the token broker pattern — issue short-lived tokens scoped to the exact capabilities needed.

-- Auth and env setup detail --
[05:00] Priya: A couple of best practices: 1) Store keys in your secret store (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), 2) CI/CD: set env var in secrets, don't check in configs, 3) Rotate keys and use scoped keys per service, 4) For E2E tests use a test key with limited quotas.
[05:28] Samir: On encryption, does Redwood support KMS integration for keys at rest and for customer-managed keys?
[05:34] Alex: For Hosted, we offer provider-managed encryption; for Private (VPC/on-prem) you can bring your own KMS or HSM integrations. We have a KMS integration guide — Priya will share.
[05:45] Samir: And audit logs? We need per-request logs for compliance.
[05:50] Priya: Yes, audit logs are available — request IDs, token metadata, model used, latency and cost metrics. For Private we can ship logs to your SIEM, or for Dedicated there's a log-forwarding option into your logging pipeline.

-- Quickstart demos and pitfalls --
[06:30] Priya: Demo time: I'll share my screen (note: transcript auto here, screen share referenced). Example app: small Flask app hitting Redwood for summarization. The repo has a Dockerfile and local dev script. We'll simulate an env with REDWOOD_API_KEY set locally.
[07:02] Priya: One common pitfall — forgetting to set MODEL_TOKEN_LIMITS or sequence length; if you pick a model with 8k context but pass 20k, you'll get truncation. We have client-side validation to warn but it's good to enforce on your side too.
[07:20] Maya: For our use case we're doing clinical note summarization — PII handling is a big thing. Do you have DLP or redaction hooks?
[07:28] Priya: We recommend pre-processing: token-level redaction before send, and we can enable retention settings per-tenant. For Private deployments we can set retention to zero and disable logging. Diego: also add prefix/KV caching rules so sensitive tokens aren't cached.

[08:10] Jordan: Performance — we need 200ms 95th for short prompts. Is that realistic?
[08:15] Priya: For small models yes. For rw-small-2k you'll likely see sub-200ms depending on region and batch settings. For dedicated you'd reserve capacity and get consistent tail latency. Our console shows per-route latency breakdown so you can tune batch windows.

-- Console & Optimize mention --
[09:05] Alex: Quick note on Console and Optimize — Console will show token-level costs and latency, Optimize suggests quantization and batching settings. For initial PoC you can use hosted and run the Optimize suggestions to reduce cost.
[09:20] Jordan: Do you have an SDK hook to fetch Optimize suggestions programmatically?
[09:25] Diego: There's an API endpoint that returns recommended config for given workload profiles; it's in the examples. Priya will send the example script.

-- Private deployment / VPC specifics --
[10:10] Samir: If we go Private, we need the service inside our VPC, with no public egress, and BYOK KMS. Also SSO and SAML for admin portal.
[10:20] Alex: Yep we support VPC private control plane with customer-managed networking. For SSO we have SAML/SCIM support for RBAC. BYOK is available in Private via KMS/HSM integrations. We'll include our SOC2 + KMS docs.
[10:35] Samir: What's the onboarding timeline for Private?
[10:38] Alex: Typical is 6-8 weeks for initial deploy and config, less if you accept our managed hosting within your cloud account. Dedicated is faster. We'll scope exact timeline in the SOW.

-- Live coding snippets and errors --
[11:15] Priya: I'm going to run the Flask example locally — note sometimes people hit 401 if they forget the header Authorization: Bearer <key>. Also content-type application/json needed for bulk calls.
[11:30] Maya: I'm seeing a redauth error in our test environment earlier — probably because our CI masks the var.
[11:35] Priya: Right, CI masking and substitution often cause that. Check pipeline logs for masked secrets and ensure the env var is present in the runner.

[12:10] Diego: Another gotcha: when doing streaming from node, ensure you use the correct transform stream helper in the SDK; otherwise you can get chunk order jitter. We log the sequence id on each chunk to help debug.

-- Questions from customer about limits and pricing --
[13:00] Jordan: Can you summarize pricing quickly? We just need the high-level tiers.
[13:05] Alex: Hosted is usage-based — per-token generation and embedding pricing. Dedicated is committed monthly capacity with discounts and SLA. Private is license + support + infra. I'll send a high-level sheet after.
[13:18] Jordan: And trial?
[13:20] Alex: We can spin up a trial with credits and a sandbox deployment, typical for PoC.

-- Security deep-dive bits --
[14:00] Samir: For SOC2 we need evidence of encryption, key rotation, pen test reports. Can you provide those?
[14:06] Alex: Yes, we'll include SOC2 Type II and our pen test summary. For dedicated/private we can provide more detailed diagrams and evidence.

-- SDK config for routing & fallbacks --
[15:05] Priya: Quick note on routing config: in the client config you can set route policy: latencyFirst or costFirst. Example: client = new Redwood({ apiKey:..., routingPolicy: 'latencyFirst' }); When capacity is tight we provide automatic fallback to cheaper model variants. We recommend testing fallback behavior in staging.
[15:35] Maya: How do you instrument that in our tracing?
[15:38] Diego: Each request emits a request_id and fallback_reason in the response metadata; we forward that into console and you can ship it to your tracing system.

-- PoC scoping conversation --
[16:10] Jordan: For the PoC we propose: ingest 10k clinical notes, run extract+summarize pipeline, measure latency and cost. Two-week timeline. Is that reasonable?
[16:22] Priya: Yes, two weeks is fine. We'll help set up the sample harness and share a benchmark script that hits the client with concurrency.
[16:30] Alex: Also recommend a small A/B to measure quality differences for quantized vs FP models — Optimize can suggest quantization profiles.

-- Hand-off and resources --
[17:05] Priya: I'll drop links: quickstart repo (github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts) — includes python/flask, node/express examples, token-broker sample, docker compose for local dev. Also sample env files (.env.example) showing REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_DEPLOYMENT_URL, REDWOOD_REGION.
[17:30] Diego: And a troubleshooting doc: common 401s, rate limits, and how to inspect request_id in console.

-- Misc clarifications and small talk --
[18:00] Jordan: What's the expected engineering effort? One sprint to wire up, another to run tests?
[18:05] Priya: Usually a small integration — 1-2 engineers for 1-2 sprints to integrate and iterate. For Private adds extra infra work.
[18:15] Tara: For infra we need Terraform modules if you have them.
[18:18] Alex: We do provide Terraform examples for Dedicated and Private to provision connectors and IAM roles. We'll share that.

-- Recap and explicit next steps --
[19:00] Alex: Quick recap: we'll send pricing and SOW, Priya will share the quickstart repo and sample scripts, Samir will confirm KMS/retention requirements, and we'll schedule the PoC kickoff for week of April 6.
[19:15] Jordan: Sounds good. Any blockers on Redwood side?
[19:18] Alex: None from our side; just waiting on your sample traffic and security sign-off to finalize SOW.

[19:40] Maya: One last technical — do you support per-tenant retention control via the SDK or is that set only on the Console?
[19:45] Priya: For hosted it's admin config in Console per workspace; for Private you can set it via API. We'll include the API docs link.

[20:10] Samir: Thanks everyone, appreciate the thoroughness.
[20:15] Alex: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials.

(Transcript notes: Auto-transcription with occasional misheard words, e.g., 'redwood' sometimes appears as 'reedwood' in the capture. Timestamps approximate every 30-90s. Screen shares and links referenced rather than pasted.)

End of meeting.
